questions.subject: history
questions.prompt: What is the 'Industrial Revolution'?
options: A period of rapid change when factories, machines and steam power transformed how things were made
A war between France and Britain
The age when humans discovered electricity for the first time
questions.answer: A period of rapid change when factories, machines and steam power transformed how things were made
questions.hint: Think factories, machines, steam, smoke.
questions.explanation: The Industrial Revolution was a period (roughly 1750–1900) when Britain (and then the world) shifted from making goods by hand at home to making them by machine in factories powered by steam.
questions.source: CHS Y8 History KM, Spring/Summer — Industrial Revolution

questions.subject: history
questions.prompt: In which country did the Industrial Revolution begin?
questions.answer: Britain
questions.hint: It started here before spreading abroad.
questions.explanation: Britain was the first country to industrialise from around 1750. It had coal, iron, trade networks, capital from empire and slavery, and a stable government — the perfect conditions.
questions.source: CHS Y8 History KM — Industrial Revolution

questions.subject: history
questions.prompt: What nickname was given to Manchester because of its huge cotton industry?
questions.answer: Cottonopolis
questions.hint: It combines 'cotton' with the Greek word for 'city' (polis).
questions.explanation: Manchester was nicknamed 'Cottonopolis' — the cotton city — because it became the world centre of cotton manufacturing in the 19th century.
questions.source: CHS Y8 History KM — Cottonopolis

questions.subject: history
questions.prompt: Which factors helped Manchester become Cottonopolis? (Select all that apply)
options: Wet climate (good for spinning cotton thread)
Coal nearby in Lancashire to power steam engines
The port of Liverpool nearby for importing raw cotton
Lots of fast-flowing rivers and streams for early water-powered mills
answer: Wet climate (good for spinning cotton thread)
Coal nearby in Lancashire to power steam engines
The port of Liverpool nearby for importing raw cotton
Lots of fast-flowing rivers and streams for early water-powered mills
questions.hint: Manchester had four big advantages and zero volcanoes.
questions.explanation: Manchester had a damp climate (great for cotton), nearby coal, the port of Liverpool for importing raw cotton from America, and fast streams to power early mills.
questions.source: CHS Y8 History KM — Cottonopolis (Manchester)

questions.subject: history
questions.prompt: What name is given to the large buildings where many workers used machines together to mass-produce goods?
questions.answer: factories
questions.hint: These replaced cottage industries — and in the cotton industry were often called 'mills'.
questions.explanation: Factories (called 'mills' in the cotton trade) brought workers together with powered machines in one building. This replaced the older 'cottage industry' where work was done at home.
questions.source: CHS Y8 History KM — Industrial Revolution

questions.subject: history
questions.prompt: Which Scottish engineer's improvements to the steam engine in the 1760s–80s helped power the Industrial Revolution?
questions.answer: James Watt
questions.hint: The unit of power is named after him.
questions.explanation: James Watt's improved steam engine (patented 1769) was much more efficient than earlier designs. It powered factories, mines and eventually trains. The 'watt' unit of power is named after him.
questions.source: UK NC KS3 — Industrial Revolution

questions.subject: history
questions.prompt: What is 'urbanisation'?
options: People moving from countryside to cities
questions.answer: People moving from countryside to cities
questions.hint: It's the growth of urban (city) areas.
questions.explanation: Urbanisation is the movement of people from rural (countryside) areas to urban (city) areas. During the Industrial Revolution, millions left farms to seek factory work in cities.
questions.source: CHS Y8 History KM — Industrial Revolution

questions.subject: history
questions.prompt: Roughly how much did Manchester's population grow during the 19th century?
options: It grew about 10 times (from 75,000 to over 700,000)
questions.answer: It grew about 10 times (from 75,000 to over 700,000)
questions.hint: Manchester's population exploded during the cotton boom.
questions.explanation: Manchester grew from around 75,000 in 1801 to over 700,000 by 1901 — a tenfold increase. Workers flooded in from rural England, Ireland and abroad seeking factory jobs.
questions.source: CHS Y8 History KM — Cottonopolis

questions.subject: history
questions.prompt: Which of these were common problems faced by workers in industrial cities? (Select all that apply)
questions.hint: Healthcare was very basic — life expectancy in industrial cities was shockingly low.
questions.explanation: Industrial cities were dangerous places. Workers faced cramped slums, polluted water (causing cholera and typhus), 12–16 hour shifts, and lethal machinery with no safety guards. Manchester's life expectancy dropped to just 26 in some areas.
questions.source: CHS Y8 History KM — Industrial Revolution social

questions.subject: history
questions.prompt: Why were children commonly employed in factories and mines during the Industrial Revolution?
options: They were paid less than adults and small enough to fit in tight spaces
It was the law that all children had to work
questions.answer: They were paid less than adults and small enough to fit in tight spaces
questions.hint: Factory owners cared about cost, and child bodies could do certain jobs.
questions.explanation: Children were employed because owners could pay them very little, and their small bodies could fit under machines, into chimneys, or down narrow mine shafts to push trucks.
questions.source: CHS Y8 History KM — Industrial Revolution

questions.subject: history
questions.prompt: What did the 1833 Factory Act do?
options: Limited working hours for children and required some schooling (no under-9s in textile mills, max 9-hour day for 9–13 year olds)
Gave women the right to vote
questions.answer: Limited working hours for children and required some schooling (no under-9s in textile mills, max 9-hour day for 9–13 year olds)
questions.hint: It was one of the first laws protecting child workers.
questions.explanation: The 1833 Factory Act banned children under 9 from working in textile mills, limited 9–13 year olds to 9 hours a day, and required factory inspectors. It was the first real step in regulating child labour.
questions.source: UK NC KS3 — Industrial Revolution

questions.subject: history
questions.prompt: Which fuel was burned to power the new steam engines and factories during the Industrial Revolution?
questions.answer: coal
questions.hint: A black rock dug from underground.
questions.explanation: Coal was the fuel of the Industrial Revolution. It powered steam engines, heated furnaces to make iron, and warmed homes. Britain had huge coal reserves.
questions.source: CHS Y8 History KM — Industrial Revolution

questions.subject: history
questions.prompt: What was the 'Spinning Jenny' invented by James Hargreaves in 1764?
options: A machine that spun multiple threads of cotton at once
questions.answer: A machine that spun multiple threads of cotton at once
questions.hint: It revolutionised the cotton industry by spinning many threads with one operator.
questions.explanation: The Spinning Jenny allowed one worker to spin 8 or more threads at once instead of just one — massively increasing cotton production. It was a key invention of the Industrial Revolution.
questions.source: CHS Y8 History KM — Industrial Revolution

questions.subject: history
questions.prompt: What was the world's first inter-city passenger railway, opened in 1830?
questions.answer: The Liverpool and Manchester Railway
questions.hint: It linked two big cities in the north-west — including Cottonopolis.
questions.explanation: The Liverpool and Manchester Railway opened in 1830, the world's first inter-city passenger railway. It connected the port (Liverpool) to Cottonopolis (Manchester) and transformed transport.
questions.source: CHS Y8 History KM — Cottonopolis

questions.subject: history
questions.prompt: What does the phrase 'Liberty's Dawn' refer to in the context of the Industrial Revolution?
options: The historian Emma Griffin's argument that industrialisation actually IMPROVED the lives of many ordinary people
The first sunrise of the 19th century
questions.answer: The historian Emma Griffin's argument that industrialisation actually IMPROVED the lives of many ordinary people
questions.hint: It's the title of a 2013 book by historian Emma Griffin.
questions.explanation: 'Liberty's Dawn' is the title of Emma Griffin's 2013 book. She used 350+ working-class autobiographies to argue that industrialisation gave many workers higher wages, more freedom and rising hopes — countering the very bleak traditional view.
questions.source: CHS Y8 History KM, Spring — Liberty's Dawn

questions.subject: history
questions.prompt: According to the 'Liberty's Dawn' interpretation, which were positive consequences of industrialisation for some working people? (Select all that apply)
options: More freedom to choose their employer
Better food and clothing as prices fell
answer: More freedom to choose their employer
Better food and clothing as prices fell
questions.hint: Voting rights came later through political reform, not industrialisation itself.
questions.explanation: Griffin argued industrialisation brought higher wages, more freedom (you could quit one job and find another), literacy through Sunday schools, and cheaper consumer goods. Voting rights came later through political struggle.
questions.source: CHS Y8 History KM, Spring — Liberty's Dawn

questions.subject: history
questions.prompt: Why might historians DISAGREE with the 'Liberty's Dawn' interpretation?
options: Average wages rose, but so did death rates, child labour, slum housing and pollution — many people's lives clearly got worse
All historians agree it was great
Workers had no jobs at all before the revolution
questions.answer: Average wages rose, but so did death rates, child labour, slum housing and pollution — many people's lives clearly got worse
questions.hint: Historians are split — Griffin's optimistic view is one of several interpretations.
questions.explanation: Critics argue average wage statistics hide the brutal reality of slums, disease, child labour and 16-hour days. Some workers gained; many — especially women, children and the unskilled — suffered terribly. Historians actively debate this.
questions.source: CHS Y8 History KM — Liberty's Dawn (interpretations)

questions.subject: history
questions.prompt: What is the link between Manchester's cotton industry and the Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade?
options: No link — Manchester cotton was grown in Yorkshire
Manchester mills processed raw cotton picked by enslaved people on plantations in the American South
Manchester sold cotton to enslaved people
questions.answer: Manchester mills processed raw cotton picked by enslaved people on plantations in the American South
questions.hint: Where did the raw cotton come from?
questions.explanation: Manchester's cotton mills depended on raw cotton from US slave plantations. So the city's prosperity was built — at least until the 1860s — on the labour of enslaved people thousands of miles away.
questions.source: CHS Y8 History KM — Cottonopolis (Manchester)

questions.subject: history
questions.prompt: During the American Civil War (1861–65), the Union blockaded the South and Manchester's cotton supply was cut off. What was the 'Lancashire Cotton Famine'?
options: A famine when Manchester workers ate cotton
A period when Manchester mills closed and workers starved, yet many still publicly supported Lincoln and the abolition of slavery
A time when no one wanted cotton clothes
questions.answer: A period when Manchester mills closed and workers starved, yet many still publicly supported Lincoln and the abolition of slavery
questions.hint: Manchester workers made a remarkable moral choice despite their own hunger.
questions.explanation: When the Union blockade cut off raw cotton, Manchester mills closed and thousands lost work. Yet in 1862 workers at the Free Trade Hall famously voted to support Lincoln and abolition — even though it harmed their own livelihoods. Lincoln wrote thanking them.
questions.source: CHS Y8 History KM — Manchester, abolition

questions.subject: history
questions.prompt: What was the name of the influential anti-slavery campaign group founded in 1787 (which Wilberforce was part of)?
questions.answer: Society for the Abolition of the Slave Trade
accepted: Society for the Abolition of the Slave Trade
Society for Effecting the Abolition of the Slave Trade
questions.hint: It has 'Society', 'Abolition' and 'Slave Trade' in the name.
questions.explanation: Founded in 1787 by Thomas Clarkson, Granville Sharp and others, the Society organised petitions, pamphlets and the famous Brookes ship diagram. Wilberforce represented them in Parliament.
questions.source: UK NC KS3 — Abolition

questions.subject: history
questions.prompt: Why was Olaudah Equiano's autobiography so powerful for the abolition movement?
options: It was the first detailed first-person account from a formerly enslaved person, written in English
questions.answer: It was the first detailed first-person account from a formerly enslaved person, written in English
questions.hint: What made his voice unique compared to white abolitionists?
questions.explanation: Equiano's 1789 autobiography 'The Interesting Narrative' was the first widely read first-person account from a formerly enslaved African in English. White readers could no longer pretend they didn't know what slavery was like.
questions.source: CHS Y8 History KM, Spring — Slave Trade/Abolition

questions.subject: history
questions.prompt: What was a 'cottage industry'?
options: A business making tiny cottage models
A system where goods (like cloth) were made by people working at home with simple tools
questions.answer: A system where goods (like cloth) were made by people working at home with simple tools
questions.hint: Cottage = small home — and it's what came BEFORE the factory.
questions.explanation: Cottage industry was the old way of producing goods at home using hand tools (spinning wheels, hand looms). The Industrial Revolution replaced it with factory production powered by machines.
questions.source: CHS Y8 History KM — Industrial Revolution

questions.subject: history
questions.prompt: What were 'Luddites'?
options: Skilled textile workers who smashed machines because they were destroying their jobs and wages (1811–16)
questions.answer: Skilled textile workers who smashed machines because they were destroying their jobs and wages (1811–16)
questions.hint: Their name is still used today for someone who hates new technology.
questions.explanation: Luddites were skilled workers who smashed knitting and weaving machines between 1811–16. The machines were replacing them and lowering wages. The government executed or transported many of them.
questions.source: UK NC KS3 — Industrial Revolution

questions.subject: history
questions.prompt: What happened at the Peterloo Massacre in Manchester in 1819?
options: Cavalry charged a peaceful crowd demanding the vote and reform, killing around 18 people and injuring 700
questions.answer: Cavalry charged a peaceful crowd demanding the vote and reform, killing around 18 people and injuring 700
questions.hint: It happened at St Peter's Field — the name is a dark joke combining 'Peter' with 'Waterloo'.
questions.explanation: On 16 August 1819 around 60,000 people gathered at St Peter's Field in Manchester to demand voting reform. Cavalry attacked the crowd, killing around 18 and injuring 700. It became a symbol of political oppression.
questions.source: CHS Y8 History KM — Manchester / Industrial Revolution political

questions.subject: history
questions.prompt: Put these Industrial Revolution inventions/events in chronological order.
questions.hint: Spinning Jenny 1764, Watt 1769, Peterloo 1819, railway 1830.
questions.explanation: Spinning Jenny (1764), Watt's steam engine (1769), Peterloo Massacre (1819), Liverpool–Manchester Railway (1830).
questions.source: CHS Y8 History KM — Industrial Revolution

questions.subject: history
questions.prompt: What is a 'slum'?
options: A very poor, overcrowded area of a city with bad housing and sanitation
questions.answer: A very poor, overcrowded area of a city with bad housing and sanitation
questions.hint: Engels described Manchester's worst neighbourhoods as some of the worst he'd ever seen.
questions.explanation: Slums were the cramped, dirty, overcrowded areas where the poorest workers lived. They often had no clean water, no sewers, and were breeding grounds for disease.
questions.source: CHS Y8 History KM — Industrial Revolution social

questions.subject: history
questions.prompt: Which German thinker wrote 'The Condition of the Working Class in England' (1845) based on his time observing Manchester's slums?
questions.answer: Friedrich Engels
questions.hint: He later co-wrote The Communist Manifesto with Karl Marx.
questions.explanation: Friedrich Engels lived in Manchester in the 1840s working for his father's textile business. His book described the appalling conditions he saw. He later co-wrote The Communist Manifesto with Karl Marx.
questions.source: UK NC KS3 — Industrial Revolution / Manchester

questions.subject: history
questions.prompt: Which disease, spread by dirty water, killed thousands in industrial cities during the 19th century?
questions.answer: Cholera
questions.hint: Doctor John Snow famously traced an outbreak to a single water pump in 1854.
questions.explanation: Cholera spreads through water contaminated by sewage. Industrial cities had no proper sewers, so outbreaks killed tens of thousands. Dr John Snow's 1854 study of a London outbreak pioneered modern epidemiology.
questions.source: CHS Y8 History KM — Industrial Revolution social

questions.subject: history
questions.prompt: Which were causes of the Industrial Revolution starting in Britain (not other countries)? (Select all that apply)
options: Wealth from colonies and the slave trade
A stable government and laws protecting business
Access to colonial markets for selling goods
answer: Wealth from colonies and the slave trade
A stable government and laws protecting business
Access to colonial markets for selling goods
questions.hint: Britain had four big advantages over rivals.
questions.explanation: Britain had coal, iron, capital from empire and slavery, a stable government, and a global empire that provided raw materials AND markets to sell finished goods to. This combination wasn't matched elsewhere until later.
questions.source: CHS Y8 History KM — Industrial Revolution causes

questions.subject: history
questions.prompt: What is a 'capitalist' in the context of the Industrial Revolution?
options: A person who lives in a capital city
A factory or business owner who invests money to make profit
questions.answer: A factory or business owner who invests money to make profit
questions.hint: Think of mill owners who invested money to make more money.
questions.explanation: A capitalist invests money (capital) to start a business — like a factory — and aims to make a profit. Factory owners are the classic example from the Industrial Revolution.
questions.source: UK NC KS3 — Industrial Revolution

questions.subject: history
questions.prompt: What name was given to the early workers' movement in the 1830s–40s that demanded voting rights for working-class men?
questions.answer: Chartism
questions.hint: Named after their 'People's Charter' of six demands.
questions.explanation: Chartism was a working-class movement built around six demands in their 'People's Charter' (1838): votes for all men, secret ballots, equal constituencies, paid MPs, no property requirement for MPs, annual elections. Most were eventually achieved.
questions.source: UK NC KS3 — Industrial Revolution political

questions.subject: history
questions.prompt: Which positive long-term consequences did the Industrial Revolution bring to Britain? (Select all that apply)
options: Higher overall wealth and wages over time
Eventually, the rise of trade unions and workers' rights
answer: Higher overall wealth and wages over time
Eventually, the rise of trade unions and workers' rights
questions.hint: The Industrial Revolution didn't end poverty — that's still a problem today.
questions.explanation: The Industrial Revolution made Britain richer overall, produced cheaper goods, built railways and canals, and led to trade unions and workers' rights. But poverty was not ended — inequality remained, and many lived in slums.
questions.source: CHS Y8 History KM — Industrial Revolution consequences

questions.subject: history
questions.prompt: Why did Parliament finally pass the Slavery Abolition Act in 1833?
options: Slave rebellions (especially in Jamaica), economic decline of plantations, mass abolitionist campaigning, AND a recent reform of Parliament made it possible
Only because the King demanded it
Because slavery had already ended naturally
Because slave owners asked for it
questions.answer: Slave rebellions (especially in Jamaica), economic decline of plantations, mass abolitionist campaigning, AND a recent reform of Parliament made it possible
questions.hint: Multiple causes combined — including the 1832 Reform Act changing who was in Parliament.
questions.explanation: The 1833 Act resulted from many causes: mass petitions, the 1831 Jamaica revolt (Baptist War), the falling profitability of Caribbean sugar, and the 1832 Great Reform Act which brought new reform-minded MPs into Parliament.
questions.source: CHS Y8 History KM — Abolition

questions.subject: history
questions.prompt: What was controversial about the 1833 Slavery Abolition Act?
options: The British government paid £20 million in compensation — to slave OWNERS, not to enslaved people
It freed slaves overnight with no problems
It only applied to British people
questions.answer: The British government paid £20 million in compensation — to slave OWNERS, not to enslaved people
questions.hint: Who got paid as a result of the Act?
questions.explanation: The 1833 Act paid £20 million (around 40% of the government's annual budget) to slave OWNERS as compensation for losing their 'property'. Enslaved people received nothing — and were forced into 'apprenticeships' before full freedom.
questions.source: CHS Y8 History KM — Abolition

questions.subject: history
questions.prompt: Why did Manchester get the nickname 'shock city' in the 19th century?
options: It grew so fast and was so unlike anywhere else (huge factories, slums, smoke and immense wealth side-by-side) that visitors were astonished
questions.answer: It grew so fast and was so unlike anywhere else (huge factories, slums, smoke and immense wealth side-by-side) that visitors were astonished
questions.hint: Historian Asa Briggs called it a 'shock city' because it shocked observers.
questions.explanation: Manchester was the first true industrial city — visitors like Alexis de Tocqueville, Engels and Dickens were astonished by its scale, its smoke, its wealth and its terrible slums. Historian Asa Briggs called it a 'shock city'.
questions.source: CHS Y8 History KM — Cottonopolis / Manchester
